corrected_value.title_o: Correcting statistical misinformation about scientific findings in the media: Causation versus correlation.

decisions.quote:

decisions.location: Abstract, p. 2, lines 14-15 (Reference list entry on p. 31, lines 564-567)
decisions.reason: The manuscript explicitly identifies Irving, Clark, Lewandowsky, and Allen (2022; DOI: 10.1037/xap0000408) as the single target of its direct replication, matching both the shipped row and blind target 0.

decisions.quote:
20   also supported the robustness of their findings to alternative modelling choices. Our findings

decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall replication verdict that their findings represent a successful direct replication of Irving et al. (2022), confirming both primary hypotheses H1 (fewer mistaken causal inferences) and H2 (more correlational inferences, albeit with a smaller effect size than the original). Under codebook Rule 1 and the 'successful' category definition, a smaller effect size on one confirmed hypothesis does not make the outcome mixed when the authors' overall verdict is successful.

decisions.quote:
14   We conducted a direct replication of Irving et al. (2022) examining whether a debunking
15   statement reduces mistaken causal inferences from correlational evidence. We randomly
16   allocated participants to read a news article containing either a correction statement (n =
17   65) or a no-correction control (n = 64).
decisions.reason: The study collected new data from 129 participants recruited via Prolific to re-test the published findings of Irving et al. (2022). Although the authors also verified computational reproducibility on the original open dataset to confirm their analysis pipeline and set informed priors, the study's primary design and contribution is a direct replication on a new sample.
